scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The name refers to the topmost rafter of a traditional house; just as that beam completes a home, this dance completes a ceremony.
This is Taualuga. Traditional (pre-colonial to present).
on_screen: Title card: Taualuga · Samoa · Traditional (pre-colonial to present)

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The term Taualuga refers to the final stage of traditional house building in Samoa, symbolizing the 'beautifying final touches' of a construction.
Historically, the dance was a sacred rite reserved for the virgins of the aristocracy, specifically the taupou (chief's daughter) or manaia (chief's son).
The taupou was protected by 'tausi' (older women) to preserve her reputation, as she was the leader of the unmarried women and the face of her village's hospitality.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: It is typically performed as the grand finale of weddings, social functions, and festivities.
It is rarely performed during religious dedications to avoid detracting from the spiritual nature of the event, though it may lead Catholic processions.
The dance signifies the conclusion of an event and the status of the performing family.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Taualuga is a solo performance characterized by graceful refinement and subtle hand and facial gestures.
The dancer maintains a stately poise while executing fluid movements.
It is often preceded by the 'ailao,' an exhibition of skill involving the twirling and throwing of a 'nifo'oti' (hooked blade).

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by choral music and simple percussion.
Traditional instruments include the slit gong or rolled mats (fala) that are beaten with sticks.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dancer wears an 'ie toga (fine mat) wrapped with a tapa sash (vala).
The body is anointed with scented coconut oil.

The most distinct element is the 'tuiga' headdress, traditionally composed of a turtle shell faceplate (lave), a headband of nautilus shells (pale fuiono), a wig of human hair (ie lau'ulu), and red feathers (ie'ula).
on_screen: Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: The performance is centered on the 'taupou' (daughter of a high chief) or the 'manaia' (son of a high chief).
The 'fuataimi' serves as the musical conductor, while the 'aiuli' or 'fa'aluma' provide the energetic, contrasting accompaniment.
While central to Samoa, the dance has been adapted across Western Polynesia.
The dance is a core component of the Fa'amatai (chiefly) system of Samoa.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Traditionally reserved for the high-born virgins of the village; it is the pinnacle of ceremonial protocol. Outsiders should treat the performance with high respect and observe the 'lafo' (money gifting) custom if appropriate.
